module_title: Valence Bond Theory, Hybridization & Dipole Moments (Intermediate)
introduction: This intermediate tier transitions from simple dot structures to the quantum mechanical treatment of bonding. It covers Valence Bond Theory (VBT), the crucial concept of Hybridization, and macroscopic molecular properties like Dipole Moment and Fajans' Rules (covalent character in ionic bonds).

core_concepts.title: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) and Overlapping
core_concepts.description:
A covalent bond is formed by the partial overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals of opposite spins. Greater overlap implies a stronger bond.
1. Sigma ($\sigma$) Bond: Formed by head-on (axial) overlapping along the internuclear axis (s-s, s-p, p-p axial). It is strong and allows free rotation.
2. Pi ($\pi$) Bond: Formed by sideways (lateral) overlapping perpendicular to the internuclear axis (p-p lateral). It is weaker and restricts rotation. A single bond is always $\sigma$, a double bond is $1\sigma + 1\pi$, a triple bond is $1\sigma + 2\pi$.

core_concepts.title: Hybridization
core_concepts.description:
The phenomenon of mixing atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the central atom to form an entirely new set of equivalent orbitals (hybrid orbitals) of identical energy and shape. This explains symmetrical geometries.
- sp: Linear ($180^\circ$), e.g., $BeCl_2$, $C_2H_2$.
- $sp^2$: Trigonal Planar ($120^\circ$), e.g., $BF_3$, $C_2H_4$.
- $sp^3$: Tetrahedral ($109.5^\circ$), e.g., $CH_4$, $H_2O$.
- $sp^3d$: Trigonal Bipyramidal ($120^\circ$ equatorial, $90^\circ$ axial), e.g., $PCl_5$.
- $sp^3d^2$: Octahedral ($90^\circ$), e.g., $SF_6$.

core_concepts.title: Dipole Moment ($\mu$)
core_concepts.description: A vector quantity measuring the polarity of a bond or a molecule. $\mu = q \times d$ (charge $\times$ distance). Unit is Debye (D). For a polyatomic molecule, the net dipole moment is the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles. If the vector sum is zero (highly symmetrical molecules like $CCl_4$, $BF_3$, $CO_2$), the molecule is Non-Polar ($\mu=0$). If the sum is non-zero (like $H_2O$, $NH_3$), the molecule is Polar.

core_concepts.title: Fajans' Rules (Covalent Character in Ionic Bonds)
core_concepts.description:
No bond is 100% ionic. Covalent character is introduced when the cation polarizes (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion. Conditions favoring high covalent character:
1. High charge on either cation or anion (e.g., $AlCl_3 > MgCl_2 > NaCl$).
2. Small size of cation (high polarizing power, e.g., $LiCl > NaCl$).
3. Large size of anion (high polarizability, e.g., $LiI > LiCl$).
4. Pseudo-noble gas configuration of cation (e.g., $Cu^+ > Na^+$).

important_entities.name: Bent's Rule (For $sp^3d$ Hybridization)
important_entities.key_fact: More electronegative atoms prefer axial positions; Lone pairs and multiple bonds prefer equatorial positions.
important_entities.significance: In Trigonal Bipyramidal ($sp^3d$) geometry, the axial bonds have less s-character and are longer/weaker. Electronegative atoms seek orbitals with less s-character, so they go axial (e.g., in $PCl_3F_2$, the F atoms occupy axial positions). Lone pairs and double bonds require more space (s-character), so they go to equatorial positions ($120^\circ$) to minimize repulsion.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very common conceptual trap. Fluorine is much more electronegative than Hydrogen, so one might guess $NF_3$ has a higher dipole moment. WRONG. In $NH_3$, the three N-H bond dipoles point UP toward Nitrogen, adding perfectly to the lone pair dipole (also pointing UP). In $NF_3$, the three N-F bond dipoles point DOWN toward Fluorine, opposing and canceling out the upward lone pair dipole. Thus, $\mu(NH_3) > \mu(NF_3)$.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Small Cat, Large Anion, Big Charge = Covalent
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To rapidly determine which compound has the lowest melting point or is most soluble in organic solvents (both properties of covalent compounds), look for the Smallest Cation, the Largest Anion, or the highest charge. Conversely, Large Cat + Small Anion = highly Ionic.

exam_strategy_tips: To quickly calculate the number of sigma and pi bonds in complex organic or inorganic structures: Number of $\sigma$ bonds = (Total number of atoms) - 1 + (Number of rings). Every subsequent bond between the same two atoms is a $\pi$ bond.
